q: What does Math dot round return for minus two point five?
o: Minus three, because it always rounds halves away from zero
Minus two, because it adds one half and takes the floor
Minus two point five, unchanged, as a double
It throws an ArithmeticException for negative halves
e: The answer is two. Math dot round adds one half and takes the floor, so minus two point five becomes minus two, while positive two point five becomes three.

q: A byte variable b holds ten. Which statement compiles without a cast?
o: A plain assignment of b plus five
Multiplying b by one and assigning it back
The compound form, b plus equals five
Unary plus, b equals plus b
e: The answer is three. Compound assignment includes an implicit cast back to the variable's type. The other forms produce an int, which can't be assigned to a byte without a cast.

q: Two Integer variables are both assigned the literal one hundred twenty-seven by autoboxing. What does comparing them with double equals give?
o: True, because small Integer values are cached
A compile error, because double equals isn't allowed on wrappers
A NullPointerException, because unboxing happens first
Always false, because they are different objects
e: The answer is one. Integer dot valueOf caches small values, so both variables point to the same object. With one hundred twenty-eight, the comparison would normally be false.

q: A String variable s holds "java". The code calls s dot toUpperCase without assigning the result, then prints s. What is printed?
o: Java, with only the first letter capitalized
Nothing, because the call fails to compile
e: The answer is four. Strings are immutable. toUpperCase returns a new String, and since the result isn't assigned, s is unchanged.

q: Which statement about text blocks is correct?
o: They keep every leading space exactly as typed in the source
Incidental indentation is removed, based on the least indented line, including the closing delimiter
They can start on the same line as the opening three quotes, like a normal string literal
They always end with a line break, whatever you do
e: The answer is two. The opening delimiter must be followed by a line break, and the common incidental indentation is stripped. Placing the closing delimiter on the last content line avoids the final line break.

q: What does Period dot ofYears one, followed by dot ofDays two, produce?
o: A period with both the years and the days
A compile error, because the methods can't be chained
A period where the years are converted into days
A period with only the days from ofDays
e: The answer is four. ofDays is a static method. Calling it on the result of ofYears ignores that result, so only the last call counts: P two D.

q: What happens when you call plusHours on a LocalDate?
o: It compiles, and throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException at runtime
It compiles, and adds the hours as a fraction of a day
It doesn't compile, because LocalDate has no plusHours method
It compiles, and returns the same date unchanged
e: The answer is three. LocalDate has no time part, so it has no plusHours method. Using plus with a time-based unit or Duration compiles, but throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException at runtime.

q: In a DateTimeFormatter pattern, what does a lowercase m mean?
e: The answer is one. Uppercase M is the month, lowercase m is the minute. Uppercase H is the hour on a twenty-four hour clock, lowercase h on a twelve hour clock.

q: Clocks in a time zone jump forward one hour at two in the morning. You create a ZonedDateTime for half past two that day. What do you get?
o: A DateTimeException, because the local time doesn't exist
An hour earlier, because the time is moved back
An hour later, with the summer offset
The same local time, with the winter offset
e: The answer is three. During a gap, the local time is moved forward by the length of the gap, so half past two becomes half past three with the summer offset.

q: A switch expression on an int value has cases for one and two, and no default. What happens?
o: It compiles, and yields zero for other values
It doesn't compile, because a switch expression must be exhaustive
It compiles, and throws an exception at runtime for any other values
It compiles only if the value is final
e: The answer is two. A switch expression must produce a value for every input. For an int, that requires a default. A switch statement on an int doesn't have that requirement.

q: In a switch expression, an arrow branch has a block body. How does the block produce its value?
o: With the break keyword followed by the value
With the last expression in the block, without a keyword
e: The answer is one. Inside a block in a switch expression, yield gives the value. return would try to return from the enclosing method, which isn't allowed there.

q: A pattern switch has case CharSequence c first, and case String s second. What happens?
o: It compiles, and strings always go to the String case
It compiles, but the String case is never reached, with a warning only
It throws a ClassCastException when a String arrives
It doesn't compile, because the String case is dominated
e: The answer is four. Every String is a CharSequence, so the first case already matches everything the second would. A dominated case label is a compile error. Put the more specific case first.

q: A pattern switch receives a null selector and has no case null. What happens?
o: It doesn't compile, because a case null is mandatory
e: The answer is four. A switch without a case null throws NullPointerException on a null selector, even with a default. Add case null, or case null comma default, to handle it.

q: Where can the pattern variable s be used after the test "if not obj instanceof String s, return"?
o: Nowhere, because the test is negated
After the if statement, for the rest of the block
Only in an else branch attached to that if statement
e: The answer is three. If the if statement returns when the test fails, the compiler knows that the test succeeded afterwards, so s is in scope after the if.

q: A parent class only has a constructor that takes a String. Its child class declares no constructor at all. What happens?
o: It doesn't compile: the default constructor calls super with no arguments
The child inherits the String constructor automatically
The code compiles, and the String parameter is null
The code compiles, but fails at runtime as soon as a child object is created
e: The answer is one. Constructors aren't inherited. The compiler-generated default constructor calls super with no arguments, which doesn't exist in the parent.

q: Java 25 allows statements before the call to super in a constructor. What can these statements do?
o: Call instance methods of the object being built
Validate arguments, and assign fields that have no initializer
Read instance fields of the object to compute the arguments for super
e: The answer is two. In the constructor prologue, you can't use this, read fields, call instance methods or return. You can compute and validate arguments, call static methods, and assign uninitialized fields.

q: A class has an overload taking a long and another taking an Integer. You call it with an int. Which one runs?
o: The one declared first in the class
The Integer version, because boxing gives an exact type
Neither, because the call is ambiguous
The long version, because widening beats autoboxing
e: The answer is four. Overload resolution prefers an exact match, then widening, then boxing, then varargs. Widening an int to a long comes before boxing.

q: A parent reference points to a child object. Both classes declare a field called name and an instance method called describe. Which are used?
o: The parent's field and the child's method
The parent's field and the parent's method
The child's field and the child's method
The child's field and the parent's method
e: The answer is one. Fields are hidden, not overridden, so the reference type decides. Instance methods are overridden, so the runtime type of the object decides.

q: A class implements two interfaces that both declare a default method with the same signature. What must happen?
o: The first interface listed wins automatically
The method from the interface declared more recently is used
The class must override the method, or it doesn't compile
The call throws an exception at runtime
e: The answer is three. The compiler can't choose, so the class must override the method. Inside, it can call one of them with the interface name, dot super, dot the method.

q: In a record's compact canonical constructor, what can you assign?
o: The fields directly, using this dot the field name, like in a class
The constructor parameters, which are then copied into the fields
Only static fields of the record
Nothing at all, because records are immutable
e: The answer is two. A compact constructor works on the parameters. The fields are final and assigned automatically at the end, so assigning this dot x doesn't compile.

q: A class directly extends a sealed class and is listed in its permits clause. Which modifier must it have?
o: abstract, so it can't be instantiated
One of final, sealed or non-sealed
None, because the permits clause is enough
static, because permitted classes must be nested
e: The answer is two. Each permitted subclass must say how the hierarchy continues: final stops it, sealed restricts it again, non-sealed reopens it. Records and enums are implicitly final.

q: A compact source file declares a main method with a String array parameter and another main with no parameters. Which one does the launcher run?
o: The one with no parameters, because it's simpler
Neither, because the file doesn't compile
The one with the String array parameter
The one declared first in the file
e: The answer is three. The launcher looks for a main with a String array first, and only uses the no-parameter one when that doesn't exist.

q: Does a multi-catch of FileNotFoundException and IOException compile?
o: No, because the two types are related by inheritance
Yes, but only with a separate finally block
Only if IOException is listed first in the multi-catch
Yes, and FileNotFoundException is handled first
e: The answer is one. Types in a multi-catch can't be subclasses of each other, because one would already cover the other.

q: In a try-with-resources statement, the try block throws an exception, and then the resource's close method also throws. What reaches the caller?
o: The exception from close, which replaces the first one
Only an Error, because two exceptions can't be in flight at once
Both exceptions, chained as cause and effect
The one from the try block, with the close exception suppressed
e: The answer is four. In try-with-resources, the primary exception is the one from the try block. Exceptions thrown while closing are added to it as suppressed.

q: Both the try block and the finally block contain a return statement. Which value does the method return?
o: It depends on whether an exception was thrown
e: The answer is two. finally runs after the try's return value is computed, and its own return replaces it. Any exception from the try block would also be discarded.

q: What happens when you call add on a list created with List dot of?
o: The element is added at the end
It returns false and leaves the list unchanged
e: The answer is four. Lists from List dot of are unmodifiable. Any add, remove or set throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime.

q: You call Arrays dot asList on a String array, then call set on the list. What happens?
o: The list changes, but the array keeps its old value
The list changes, and so does the original array
It doesn't compile, because the list is read only
e: The answer is three. Arrays dot asList returns a fixed-size list backed by the array. set works and writes through to the array, while add and remove throw.

q: Which of these is a SequencedCollection, with getFirst and reversed?
e: The answer is one. LinkedHashSet has a defined encounter order, so it's sequenced. HashSet and PriorityQueue don't have a defined iteration order.

q: On a List of Integer holding ten, twenty and thirty, what does calling remove with the int literal one do?
o: It doesn't compile, because the call is ambiguous
It removes nothing, because there's no element equal to one
It removes the element at index one, which is twenty
It removes the first element, ten
e: The answer is three. remove with an int argument chooses the index version, without boxing. To remove by value, pass an Integer object.

q: A method parameter is a List of question mark extends Number. What can the method do with it?
o: Add Integers and Doubles to it
Read elements as Number, but add nothing except null
e: The answer is two. With an upper bounded wildcard, the real list could be of Integer or of Double, so adding is unsafe. Reading as Number always works. Producer extends, consumer super.

q: What must be true for Arrays dot binarySearch to give a meaningful result?
o: The array must be sorted in ascending order first
The array must contain no duplicate values
The array must hold objects, not primitives
The array must have been created with Arrays dot asList
e: The answer is one. On an unsorted array the result is undefined. When the value isn't found, the result is minus the insertion point, minus one, so a value that would go at index two gives minus three.

q: A stream pipeline has a filter and a peek that prints, but no terminal operation. What is printed?
o: Each element that passes the filter
e: The answer is four. Intermediate operations don't run until a terminal operation starts the pipeline.

q: What happens if you call count twice on the same stream object?
o: Both calls return the same result
e: The answer is four. A stream can only be consumed once. A second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException at runtime.

q: Collectors dot toMap is used with a key function and a value function, and two elements produce the same key. What happens?
o: The first value is kept, and the second is dropped
The later value replaces the earlier one
Both values are stored in a list
e: The answer is three. Without a merge function, a duplicate key throws IllegalStateException. Add a third argument, a merge function, to combine the values.

q: What does allMatch return on an empty stream?
e: The answer is one. allMatch and noneMatch return true on an empty stream, because no element fails. anyMatch returns false.

q: What does the windowFixed gatherer with a size of two produce for the numbers one to five?
o: Two windows, and the fifth number is dropped
Three windows: one-two, three-four, and five on its own
An exception, because five isn't a multiple of two
Overlapping windows: one-two, two-three, three-four, four-five
e: The answer is two. windowFixed groups elements into lists of the given size, and the last window may be shorter. windowSliding gives overlapping windows.

q: What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet on an Optional?
o: orElseGet only works on Optionals of numbers
orElse throws an exception when the Optional is empty, while orElseGet returns null
orElse always evaluates its argument; orElseGet runs its supplier only when empty
e: The answer is four. The argument to orElse is evaluated before the call, even when a value is present. orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only if needed.

q: What happens if you call run instead of start on a Thread object?
o: The task runs on the current thread, and no new thread is created
It throws IllegalThreadStateException, because the thread isn't started yet
A new thread is started, as with start
It doesn't compile, because run is protected
e: The answer is one. run is an ordinary method call. Only start creates a new thread of execution.

q: A shared counter is declared volatile, and several threads increment it with plus plus. Is the result reliable?
o: Yes, because volatile makes the increment atomic
Yes, as long as there are fewer than ten threads
No, because volatile guarantees visibility, not atomicity
No, because volatile variables can't be incremented
e: The answer is three. An increment is a read, an add and a write, and other threads can interleave. Use AtomicInteger or a lock.

q: A task submitted to an ExecutorService throws an exception. What does Future dot get do?
o: Throws ExecutionException, with the original exception as its cause
Rethrows the original exception directly, without wrapping it in anything
e: The answer is two. get wraps the task's failure in an ExecutionException, a checked exception. getCause returns the original.

q: What happens when you call setDaemon false on a virtual thread?
o: The virtual thread becomes a user thread, and keeps the JVM alive until it ends
It throws IllegalArgumentException: virtual threads are always daemons
e: The answer is two. Virtual threads are always daemon threads. Calling setDaemon with false throws IllegalArgumentException. Their priority is also fixed.

q: You call get on a ScopedValue outside any where binding. What happens?
o: It returns the value bound most recently by any thread
It blocks until a value is bound
e: The answer is three. An unbound scoped value has no value. get throws NoSuchElementException, isBound returns false, and orElse gives a fallback.

q: Why does ExecutorService work well with try-with-resources since Java 19?
o: It's AutoCloseable, and close waits for submitted tasks to finish
Its close method interrupts all tasks immediately
It closes the threads at once but keeps the task queue for later use
It doesn't; executors must be shut down manually
e: The answer is one. close shuts the executor down and waits until all tasks have completed, which makes the try-with-resources pattern simple and safe.

q: In module-info dot java, what do the requires and exports directives refer to?
o: requires names a package, and exports names a module
requires names a module, and exports names a package
e: The answer is four. You depend on modules, but you make packages accessible. A classic trap in options that export a module name.

q: What does requires transitive add to a plain requires?
o: The dependency becomes optional at runtime
Modules that read this module can also read the dependency
The dependency's packages are opened for reflection
The dependency is loaded before this module
e: The answer is two. With requires transitive, the dependency is implied readability for any module that requires this one. requires static is the optional one.

q: A file imports module java dot base and module java dot desktop, then uses the simple name List. What happens?
o: It compiles, and List means java dot util dot List, because java dot base is listed first
It compiles, and the first import wins
It compiles, and List means java dot awt dot List
It doesn't compile, because List is ambiguous between java dot util and java dot awt
e: The answer is four. Both modules export a type called List. A single-type import, or a wildcard import of java dot util, resolves the ambiguity, because both shadow module imports.

q: What does BufferedReader dot readLine return when the end of the file is reached?
e: The answer is three. readLine returns null at the end of the stream, so the classic loop reads while the line isn't null. The basic read method returns minus one.

q: What does Files dot copy do when the target file already exists and no options are given?
e: The answer is one. Without StandardCopyOption dot REPLACE_EXISTING, copy refuses to overwrite and throws FileAlreadyExistsException.

q: A serializable class has a transient int field set to five. After serializing and deserializing the object, what does the field hold?
o: Five, because the constructor runs again during deserialization
Five, because transient only affects equals
Zero, the default value, since the field isn't written
The field is missing, and reading it throws an exception
e: The answer is three. Transient fields aren't serialized, and the serializable class's constructor and initializers don't run on deserialization, so the field gets its default value.

q: You request a resource bundle for Locale fr CA, and the default locale is en US. After Messages underscore fr underscore CA and Messages underscore fr, which file is tried next?
o: The base bundle, Messages, with no locale
The bundle for the default locale, English US
The English bundle, without a country
A bundle for the country Canada only
e: The answer is two. The lookup tries the requested locale, then its language, then the default locale with its country, then the default language, and finally the base bundle.

e: The answers are 1 and 3. A qualified export names a package and the modules allowed to use it, and opens makes a package available for deep reflection. requires takes a module name without wildcards, exports takes a package, and provides needs a with clause naming the implementation.

e: The answer is 1. The consumer declares uses with the service interface. Providers declare provides, the interface, with, and the implementation class. ServiceLoader is in java.base, which every module reads.
